column5: This English volume is an edited condensation (Lawrence Hill, 1974/1978) of two French works, Nations negres et culture (1954/55) and Anteriorite des civilisations negres (1967); linguistic and technical parts are left out (translator's preface). Diop's preface says L'Afrique Noire precoloniale aimed to show laws of African socio-political evolution and that his conception had 'practically triumphed': a self-assessment, not a finding. Useful for Module 1 as history of African historiography.

Diop's argument rests on Greek and biblical witnesses (Herodotus, Diodorus, Strabo, Maspero's summary, Genesis 'Ham'). Strong: shows classical writers placed Egypt and Ethiopia in close contact and that the 'Hamite' category was built to explain civilisation away from Black Africans (he says experts cannot place Hamites by place, language or route; mainstream agrees the Hamitic hypothesis is discredited). Weak: skin-colour words in ancient Greek ('melas') are not a race measure; Diodorus reports an Ethiopian claim, not his own view; Diop treats Genesis genealogy as ethnology. Teach as a case of reading ancient written sources critically, with both sides.

Diop writes that in Herodotus's time (5th century BCE) Egyptian civilisation was 'already more than 10,000 years old'. Mainstream Egyptology dates unification to c. 3100 BCE and Old Kingdom pyramids to c. 2600 BCE (the book's own picture caption dates Chephren c. 2600 BCE), about 2,600 years before Herodotus. The 10,000-year figure is a claimed premise, not supported; do not repeat it. Note the book gives no date basis here.

Argues monotheism and Akhenaten-era religion in Egypt came from the 'Meroitic Sudan', and that Greek assimilation under Ptolemies shows Egyptians were originally Black because 'mixing' left them Black. The inference (if originally white, they would have stayed white) is not an argument historians accept (it presumes fixed racial blocks). Mention only as an example of Diop's reasoning in Module 2; label [CONTESTED].

Passage on the origin of the Jewish people and the 'curse of Ham' contains sweeping claims about Hebrew history ('rough fearful shepherds', no social organisation) with no archaeological support in the text; these are not teachable as fact. Course does not cover; note as an unsupported excursion.

Diop gives Egyptian civilisation 'presumably' 10,000 years as a 'compromise' between a long chronology from priests, Herodotus and Manetho (17000 BCE) and the modern short one (a calendar by 4245 BCE). Archaeology and radiocarbon support Egyptian state formation c. 3100 BCE; Manetho's and Herodotus's figures are priestly tradition, not data. The 4245 BCE calendar date is also questioned by mainstream chronology. Trust radiocarbon-based chronology; show Diop's figure as his own estimate, tagged [THIN EVIDENCE]/not supported.

Claims that gunpowder was known to Egyptian priests and used in religious rites (citing de Pauw, 1773) and that Africa lost out for lack of cannon. No archaeological evidence for Egyptian gunpowder; gunpowder is generally traced to China. Do not teach as fact. Also asserts 15th-century African political systems were equal or superior to European ones with 'constitutional' monarchies and a People's Council; this is a thesis (see Diop Precolonial Black Africa ch. 4), not a finding, and Module 4/5 should tag it [CONTESTED].

Diop's explanatory story: Egypt's isolation from the rest of Black Africa, then technical vs social development (Nile valley demanded geometry and irrigation; elsewhere less need). This is a speculative environmental-determinist argument, an inference by Diop. Also claims Africans 'first discovered iron' (course: independent invention is [CONTESTED]). Cites Volney (1780s) on the Sphinx and Copts as an eyewitness to Black Egyptians; useful as a primary example of how a 18th-century observer was cited (Volney's Copt description is about the people he met, then argued back to ancient Egyptians).

Diop recounts how Champollion-Figeac, Cherubini, Fontanes and Maspero dismissed a Black Egypt, and criticises their reasoning ('inadmissible', 'dark red', skin colour and hair not enough). Strong: nineteenth-century Egyptology did carry racial assumptions (the Hamitic idea, Lepsius's canon). Weak: Diop argues from the tomb relief of four peoples that the two darkest groups are both Black Africans; mainstream reading is four peoples (Egyptians, Asiatics, Nubians, Libyans) with conventional colours, so colour alone does not settle identity. Useful for a Module 1 lesson on how colour in ancient art can and cannot be read.

Diop treats Amelineau's Abydos kings (Umm el-Qaab) as pre-Menes and quotes Maspero's shifting datings to argue the establishment was evasive. Mainstream: these are First Dynasty and Dynasty 0 tombs (c. 3100 BCE onward), dated by later work. Reasoning uses an old dispute that later archaeology resolved; flag as dated. Also uses Saharan rock art (ram-headed Amon, Capsian) as evidence of a Black civilisation in Egypt's prehistoric source; the course's Sahara green-period material (Module 3/olivier glossary) supports a pastoral Sahara but not Diop's ethnic reading.

Reductio on Berber grammar and Vandals (feminine endings and plurals shared with German and Latin) is a rhetorical point about weak linguistic comparisons, and it is itself the kind of comparison that historical linguists reject (chance resemblances). Good teaching contrast for Module 1 linguistics blind spot: shared forms need regular sound correspondences.

Diop reads Narmer's palette (Hierakonpolis) as Black rulers over white or Asian captives, and compares Pharaonic regalia (ox-tail, amulet sachet, sandal-bearer) to Wolof and Nigerian practice, with Wolof word matches (dakk, bek-neg). Mainstream reading: unification of Upper and Lower Egypt under Narmer c. 3100 BCE; the regalia parallels are cultural comparisons that could show shared African substrate, but isolated word and object matches do not prove descent. Both can be shown side by side: Diop strong on pointing to African parallels (a point later Egyptologists like those who see Egypt as African in its culture also accept), weak on inferring a single Black race and ancestry.

Claims Osiris was a historic Black ancestor whose tomb Amelineau found at Abydos and that gods were painted black 'in the image of their race'. Mainstream: the Abydos tomb he excavated was of early kings (a later cult site called the tomb of Osiris), and Osiris's black or green skin is a symbol of the fertile Nile silt and rebirth. A historic Osiris is unsupported; tag [CONTESTED] and do not teach as fact.

Diop argues Egyptian civilisation arose in Upper Egypt (Nile valley) not the Delta, since Delta finds are later. Mainstream today: Upper Egypt (Hierakonpolis, Abydos, Naqada) is the core of state formation, so Diop's southern-origin point is in line with current archaeology, though the Delta (Buto, Maadi) had its own early cultures; strong on this narrow point. Much of the argument is from Greek and Egyptian myth and from Amelineau's claimed find of Osiris's head, which Diop himself says may not be authentic.

Diop asserts step pyramids at Saqqara, Babylon, in the Ivory Coast (as bronze weights) and Mexico prove Black emigration, and that Mesopotamian 'royal tombs' held no kings. Pyramids in Mesoamerica and Mesopotamia (ziggurats) are independent forms with no demonstrated link; the Ur tombs' occupants are debated but attested rulers appear in Mesopotamian king lists. Unsupported by evidence given; do not teach. Relevant to Module 8 Atlantic contact caution.

Diop derives Paris from Per-Isis, links Wolof, Egyptian, Breton, Irish and Latin words (ker, dun, Mac, Rex, Magan), and links Menes to a Wolof word for breast and matrilineal rule. Chance resemblances among short words are what historical linguists reject; no regular sound correspondences are shown. The Parisii are a Gaulish tribe. Reject as method; use as a worked example of the linguistics blind spot in Module 1 lesson 1 (shared vocabulary needs regular correspondences).

Chapter includes sweeping racial stereotypes of Jews and of 'the white world', a claim of a 'Kushite Empire' across Arabia and Babylon, and claims that Phoenician tombs would show Negro skulls ('better not to touch them'). These rest on nineteenth-century race typology (Sergi, Lenormant) and have no support in modern archaeology or genetics. Do not teach any of it; log honestly in the notes as Diop's weakest passages and as period race-science.

Diop's two-cradle theory (Southern cradle: gentle, matriarchal, agricultural; Northern cradle: harsh, nomadic, patriarchal) is introduced here. It is an environmental-deterministic generalisation, not tested; tag [CONTESTED]. Include in a Module 1 box on contested frameworks for the history of historiography, with the mainstream view that such cradles are not supported by archaeology or genetics.

The ebook text of this volume has missing and run-together passages (paragraphs cut mid-argument, captions and footnote fragments inline, chapters starting mid-sentence), so some arguments cannot be followed in full. Anything taught from it needs the passage re-read first and should be flagged as read from a damaged edition. Do not quote.

Diop argues skull measurements (Naqada crania, nasal index) give mixed results and that anthropologists never proved a white Egypt; quotes Breasted's racial statement that the Sahara barred Black peoples from civilisation. Strong: Breasted's claim is a racial assumption, and Sahara was a corridor rather than barrier in the green-Sahara period (course Module 3, Olivier ch. 9 describing Tassili). Weak: skull indices are not valid race tests; modern work uses cranial and dental affinity studies and aDNA showing Egyptians genetically closest to Near Eastern and North African populations with some sub-Saharan input, which neither Diop nor Breasted anticipated; label recent aDNA (2017 Abusir el-Meleq study) as outside these books, not verified here.

Uses ritual regicide ('Sed festival' as a symbolic replacement of killing the old king, citing Seligman 1934), cosmological claims that Dogon knew Sirius, and 'divine kingship' unity of Egypt and Black Africa. The ritual-killing reading of the Sed festival is rejected by Egyptologists; the Dogon-Sirius claim is widely doubted (Griaule's informants, possible modern influence). Teach only as a historiographic example: Frazer-Seligman comparative method, now abandoned.

Gives a vitalist theory of kingship and a matrilineal-succession claim (Ghana, Mali), and notes Kati (Tarikh al-Fattash) admitting earlier chapters 'mendacious' for lack of sources. That last point is a nice source-critique point for Module 4 lesson 3 on the Askia chronicle; the broader vitalist theory is Diop's generalisation, [CONTESTED].

Diop says Axum is 'more a word than a reality' with only one obelisk and two statue pedestals, and that temples and pyramids occur exclusively in the Meroitic Sudan (84 pyramids). Course Module 2 (Aksum: coins, Ge'ez-Sabaean-Greek inscriptions, stelae up to about 24 m, Adulis in the Periplus) shows Aksum is richly attested; Diop's statement is an error or a strawman and should be corrected. His count of 84 Meroitic pyramids differs from the course's 'over 200 approximate' (course figure is for all Sudan; the book counts only Meroe), so show both and say the totals depend on which sites are included.

Diop reads Kemit as 'land of the Blacks' (people) and says the Egyptians called themselves 'Black' (khem). Mainstream Egyptology reads Kmt as 'the black land' after the fertile Nile silt (versus red desert); the term is not a statement about the people's skin. Both readings exist; the geographic reading is the standard one and is better supported by the paired term Deshret (red land). Tag Diop's reading [CONTESTED]. Strong point: he is right that Egyptian texts have no concept of Black Africans as a separate race, and that nineteenth-century translators of Nehesy/Kush used race categories.

Quotes Ibn Battuta's praise of Mali's justice and security (no fear of brigands; property of deceased foreigners safe) and his displeasure at the Walata farba's treatment of white merchants, and Delafosse on Mali negotiating with the King of Portugal. Confirms course Module 4 l2 (Ibn Battuta praised justice and safety while criticising some customs). Diop uses it to rebut the colonial claim that Africa was insecure before colonisation: a point of argument, with the correct caution that Ibn Battuta is one visitor with a stake.

Diop proposes a 'hieroglyphic baobab' at Diourbel and argues writing may be found under African soil. Anecdote from his youth with no examination; treat as unsupported. Also argues Egyptians and Meroitic Sudanese 'belonged to the same race' and hair/prognathism show Black origin of mummies. Counterpoint: mummy hair varies and race cannot be read from prognathism; show as contested.

Diop (via Lucas, Pedrals and name comparisons) derives the Yoruba, Serer, Toucouleur, Peul and Laobe from the Nile valley: Yoruba 'agûto' sheep from Greek Aigyptos, Serer Rog with Egyptian Ra, ethnonyms Kan/Kara/Nyoro matched by sound across thousands of kilometres. These are chance resemblances among short words and place names with no regular sound correspondences, and the Yoruba-Egypt link is not accepted by linguists or archaeologists. Course Module 5 already treats the Oduduwa/Ife origin as a founding myth and Nok-Yoruba as [CONTESTED]; add Diop's Nile-origin thesis as another unproven origin claim to test with the myth checklist.

Quotes Dr Maes (1920s) saying the upright stones of Tundi-Daro could not have been made by Black Africans because only eating and sex interest them; Diop rightly exposes this as racial prejudice behind colonial refusals to credit African monuments. Parallels the course Module 7 Great Zimbabwe myth (Rhodesian claims of Phoenician builders). Strong confirmation for Module 7 lesson on the colonial myth; Maes quote is racist and should not be reproduced beyond a short paraphrase.

The chapter heading is 'Arguments Opposing a Negro Origin', yet the surviving text mostly lists name-matching and a legend of the Nile origin of peoples; Diop's migration-from-the-Nile model contrasts with the Bantu expansion evidence in Module 1 (Cameroon/Nigeria borderland origin, several waves). Where they differ, trust linguistics/archaeology of Bantu expansion; Diop's model is a hypothesis.

Diop follows Pirenne's account of Piankhi (Piye): campaign from Napata, sieges at Hermopolis, Memphis, crowned at Heliopolis, and successor Shabaka, ending the Delta rebel lords. Consistent with course lesson 1 (Piye c. 744 to 714 BCE conquers Egypt, 25th Dynasty to 656 BCE). Diop gives the 26th Dynasty from 663 BCE (course: Kushites driven out by 656 BCE); the 7-year difference reflects different chronologies for Psamtik's rise, so keep 'about' and tag dates approximate. Diop also credits the first Egyptian unification to Nekhen (Hierakonpolis) in the south, matching current archaeology.

Diop calls Narmer/Menes, Djoser and the Fourth Dynasty pyramid builders 'Negro' on the strength of statue faces and cites Petrie that the First Dynasty was Sudanese-Nubian. Petrie's 'dynastic race' theory is outdated; facial features of Old Kingdom statues are conventions and cannot give race. Tag [CONTESTED]; do not teach as fact. The Harris Papyrus temple-slave figures he quotes (e.g. 86,436 at Thebes) are quoted from Pirenne and I cannot check them; also treat his comparison of Egyptian labour to capitalism as an analogy, not a finding.

Diop asserts that Greek science and gods derived from Egypt (citing Herodotus) and that the Greek miracle is a myth; also repeats the Dogon-Sirius claim. Strong: Herodotus himself says Greek god names came largely from Egypt, and Egyptian influence on Greek culture is accepted though scale is debated (Black Athena debate, outside these books). Weak: sweeping claim that Black people invented all science, medicine, writing, religion. Use in a Module 1 side-by-side box on contested claims in the history of historiography.

Diop's reply reports the criticism by the historian Raymond Mauny and an interview remark attributed to him that the melanin test (ultraviolet and enzyme argument) shows mummies are Black; Diop says the enzyme wording came from a journalist, not from his book, but he stands by the idea that mummy skin pigment was analysed and kept at IFAN. Mauny cites Coon that Egyptians were Mediterranean with some Negro contribution. Mainstream view: skin pigment of mummies cannot be tested reliably (embalming and ageing alter it), and melanin level does not prove ancestry; modern ancient-DNA studies have not settled the question for the whole of Egypt. Present both: Diop's melanin test is a strong claim with weak support; the mainstream critique of colour-reading is stronger.

Diop's 'Reply' states an important methodological position: African historiography must be written by Africans, textbooks revised only if Egyptologists agree (his critic Mauny wrote that textbooks change only when Egyptologists confirm). Good evidence for a Module 1 box 'a debate inside African historiography in 1960s': Mauny as European historian criticising 'Negro Gobinism' (his phrase as quoted); Diop answering. Be careful: quote only short phrases.

Diop says Genesis does not call Ham's descendants black, that the Egyptians never stopped being Negroes though lightened by mixing, and argues geometry and centralised state arose from Nile flood conditions (not special racial genius). The environmental explanation (flood management, geometry) is a standard hydraulic argument also found in mainstream accounts; the racial conclusion is not.

Diop argues that Grimaldi and Cro-Magnon-era skeletons, Kenyan skeletons and the Masai are 'Negro' by cranial and nasal features, citing Boule and Vallois, Haddon, Elliot Smith and Sergi, and that steatopygia comes from carrying babies. This applies early-twentieth-century race typology (skull indices, 'Eurafrican race', 'brown race') that modern physical anthropology and genetics abandoned; Grimaldi and 'Negroid' labels are not supported by current aDNA. Do not teach. Useful only for the history of race science in historiography.

Diop describes the UNESCO General History of Africa plan (Paris, April-May 1971) and his three preconditions for volume II (African Antiquity): an Egyptologists-and-Africanists colloquium on the ancient Egyptians' anthropology, a commission on Egyptian and other African languages, and the decipherment of Nubian/Meroitic writing (meetings scheduled Cairo, November 1973). Useful Module 1/2 context: the debate was taken to a UNESCO scholarly forum; the outcome of the colloquium is not in this book (not verified here). Diop also says he never rewrites published works, preferring new publications: a method point.

Diop argues the Aurignacian came into Europe from North Africa with 'Negroid' Grimaldi people, that Cro-Magnon was the White prototype, and that Africa is the cradle of humanity. The last point is firmly established (the course Module 1 does not cover deep prehistory but nothing here conflicts); the Negroid-Aurignacian conquest of Europe is rejected by current archaeology and ancient-DNA research. Treat as outdated race typology.

Chapters XIII and the Conclusion in this ebook repeat the same long passages (Sergi/Elliot Smith/Haddon, steatopygia, Cornevin) and the beginning of Chapter XIII starts mid-quotation: the edition shows duplicated and misplaced paragraphs. Read from a defective edition; confirm anything taught against another copy of the translation before quoting.

Notes cite Leo Frobenius (Mythologie de l'Atlantide, 1949; Histoire de la civilisation africaine, 1938) as support in Chapter VII. Module 5 rejects Frobenius's 1910 claim that Ife heads came from Atlantis or the Mediterranean. Diop uses Frobenius selectively, as an early European who praised African civilisation; his Atlantis framing is the same source the course rejects. Show the point: the same source can be cited for opposed purposes; check what claim is being borrowed.

Notes give the sources of the book's evidence: Herodotus in the 1928 Rawlinson translation, Diodorus (Oldfather 1935), Maspero (1894), Moret and Davy (1923), Breasted (1926), Pedrals (1950), Delafosse (1922), Cailliaud (1836), Frobenius, Gobineau. Nearly all pre-1950, so Diop's evidence base is dated; modern work (aDNA, Egyptology after 1960) is absent. Footnote 2 to Chapter VI says black skin with woolly hair without other 'Negro' features is 'scientifically nil': an assertion, not a test.

Diop notes no known document authorises a marriage of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, only a laconic biblical visit, so the Solomonic descent claimed by Ethiopian emperors cannot be taken as history. Agrees with the course's treatment of the Kebra Nagast as a legitimising story (Module 2 lesson 4). Diop uses it to argue the later 'mixture' of Ethiopian rulers came much later, which is his own inference.

column4: ch-019 (Additional Chapter Notes, note 3 to Chapter IX)
column5: Diop quotes Edouard Schuré (1908) at length: a prehistoric Black world empire with gigantic cities, iron weapons and bronze armour that invaded southern Europe and enslaved Whites. This is occult-historical fantasy with no archaeological basis; its approving quotation in the book shows how far some of the evidence leans on unreliable nineteenth-century secondary writers. Do not teach.

Quotes Cailliaud's 1836 view that Ethiopia/Nubia has priority over Egypt (observed monuments in Nubia) with the caveat that Lower Nubia's monuments are later than Thebes. Shows that early explorers argued from direction of river and monuments; the later Nubian archaeology (Kerma, A-Group, Qustul) is not in the book. Course Module 2 starts Kerma c. 2500 BCE and Napata from 8th century BCE: Kush is old but not older than Egyptian unification as Cailliaud thought. Useful historiography example.

Bibliography lists Diop's own 1973 'on press' papers on the melanin test of Egyptian pigmentation, on iron metallurgy under the Egyptian Old Kingdom, and on the Nilotic cradle of the Senegalese people: these are the sources of his three most contested claims and the book only summarises them. It also lists a pyramidology title (Seiffert, Great Pyramid, Proof of God) and Schure's Les Grands Inities, alongside serious works (Gardiner, Pirenne, Monod, Snowden Blacks in Antiquity 1970, Davidson). Mauny identified as Director of Archaeology at IFAN: his debates with Diop were between professionals.
